what: Push notifications let your server wake a phone with a short message even when the app is closed. FCM (Firebase Cloud Messaging) carries them to Android, and APNs (Apple Push Notification service) carries them to iOS; each device gets a token that your server stores.
like: Like a doorbell with a number on it: the post office (FCM or APNs) knows the number, you just give them the number and the message.
why: Re-engage users with alerts like payment received or login attempt
Works when the app is closed, using the OS delivery channel
One server call can target a single device, a topic, or many devices

steps.d: Android 13 (API 33) made POST_NOTIFICATIONS a runtime permission, off by default for new installs. Call requestPermissions after a user action or a short explainer, not at first launch.
After permission, register() returns an FCM token on Android and an APNs-backed token on iOS through the registration event.

steps.t: Send the token to your server
steps.d: Upload it with the signed-in user and device id, and refresh it on each launch. The server keeps a last-seen timestamp.

steps.t: Server sends through FCM or APNs
steps.d: On an event your backend calls the FCM HTTP v1 API (which also reaches iOS via APNs) with the token or a topic.
pushNotificationReceived fires in the foreground; pushNotificationActionPerformed fires on tap, and that handler hands a deep link to the router.
Delete tokens FCM reports as UNREGISTERED (HTTP 404) and run a job that drops tokens not seen inside your window.

numbers.l: Android 13 is where POST_NOTIFICATIONS became a runtime permission

token refresh balances battery and stale detection; more often than weekly gives no benefit
Android 8.0 is where notification channels start

choices.d: Notification messages are shown by the OS. Data-only messages let the app decide, but on Android pushNotificationReceived does not fire if the app was killed unless you add a native FirebaseMessagingService.
Topics fit broadcasts like market news. Account events like a login alert need per-user tokens so the server controls who gets what.
Pre-prompt with your own explainer screen and trigger the system dialog from a user action. A denial is hard to undo.
Keep it generic, such as You have a new payment, and fetch details after the user opens and authenticates. Lock screens and logs can expose payloads.

instead.why: Web push for installed PWAs, using the Push API and a service worker instead of FCM native tokens
Realtime updates while the app is open, with no OS delivery involved

breaks.d: The system dialog appears before the user sees any value.
breaks.see: Low opt-in and a permanent denial
breaks.fix: Ask in context after a user action, with an explainer screen first

breaks.d: Tokens are never removed after uninstall or inactivity.
breaks.see: Rising send errors and wasted sends
breaks.fix: Delete on UNREGISTERED and prune by last-seen window

breaks.d: Balances or codes are sent in the notification body.
breaks.fix: Send an opaque id; load details after authentication

say: I request notification permission in context, because on Android 13 it is a runtime permission and a denial is hard to reverse.
I store the FCM or APNs token per user and device with a last-seen time, refresh it monthly, and delete tokens FCM reports as unregistered.
Payloads stay generic; tapping the push deep-links into the app, which authenticates before showing anything sensitive.

followups.q: What about silent pushes on iOS?
followups.a: The Capacitor plugin does not support iOS remote background push, so design so that a normal visible notification or a fetch on open covers critical updates.

followups.q: How do you handle the user denying permission?
followups.a: Keep working without push, offer an in-app inbox, and show a settings shortcut with an explanation when they later choose to enable it.

today: Android 13+ requires an explicit permission and a good prompt strategy matters more than the plumbing. FCM guidance now centres on tracking token freshness and pruning stale registrations.
